lead: Disk structure determines how fast a storage device can serve data. The geometry of a magnetic disk creates two delays: the time to move the read/write head (seek time) and the time for the desired sector to rotate under the head (rotational latency). Scheduling the order of pending I/O requests reduces these delays, improves throughput and shortens response time. Disk scheduling is used in every OS that manages hard‑disk or SSD queues, from smartphones handling UPI transaction logs to servers storing IRCTC booking data.
prereq: You need: basic file concepts from 5.1 and I/O hardware basics from 5.7.

blocks.text: A magnetic disk consists of several platters stacked on a spindle. Each platter has two surfaces that are divided into concentric tracks. A set of tracks with the same radius on all surfaces forms a cylinder. The smallest addressable unit on a surface is a sector, typically 512 bytes. The total number of cylinders, tracks per surface and sectors per track define the disk geometry.

items: Cylinders: vertical stacks of tracks; used by the OS to calculate seek distance.
Tracks per surface: determines linear distance the head travels.
Sectors per track: affect angular spacing of sectors. More sectors reduce the time to reach a particular sector after rotation starts, but the average rotational latency remains half a full rotation.

blocks.text: Access time = Seek time + Rotational latency + Transfer time
blocks.where: Seek time is the time to move the head between cylinders; Rotational latency is half a rotation on average; Transfer time is the time to read/write the sector data.

sections.h3: Seek time, rotational latency and transfer time

blocks.text: Seek time grows roughly linearly with the number of cylinders crossed. Manufacturers quote an average seek (e.g., 8 ms for a 10 000‑cylinder drive). Rotational latency depends on the spindle speed. A 7200 rpm disk completes one revolution in 8.33 ms, so the average latency is half of that, about 4.17 ms. Transfer time equals (Sector size ÷ Data rate). Transfer time (seconds) = Sector size (bytes) ÷ Data rate (bytes per second). For a 512‑byte sector on a 100 MB/s interface, transfer time is 0.005 ms, negligible compared with seek and latency.
Average seek = total head movement ÷ number of requests
blocks.where: total head movement is the sum of cylinder distances the head travels while serving all pending requests; number of requests is the count of I/O operations in the queue.

blocks.text: The OS can reorder pending requests before sending them to the disk. Different ordering policies aim to minimise the total head movement, reduce average seek, or guarantee fairness. The most common algorithms are:

items: FCFS – First‑Come‑First‑Served. Simple but can cause long seeks.
SSTF – Shortest Seek Time First. Picks the nearest request, may starve far cylinders.
SCAN – The head moves in one direction serving requests until the end, then reverses (like an elevator).
C‑SCAN – After reaching the last cylinder, the head jumps back to the start without servicing, providing uniform wait time.
LOOK and C‑LOOK – Variants that reverse at the last request instead of the physical end.
Compute the distance from the current head position to each pending request.
Select the request according to the algorithm’s rule.
Move the head, add the distance to the total movement, remove the request from the queue.
Repeat until the queue is empty.

blocks.where: movement_i is the cylinder distance covered for the i‑th request; N is the total number of requests.

examples.question: A disk head is positioned at cylinder 50. The pending I/O requests are at cylinders 55, 58, 39, 18 and 90. Compute (a) the total head movement and average seek for FCFS, and (b) the total head movement and average seek for SCAN assuming the initial direction is outward (toward larger cylinder numbers).
steps: For SCAN, move outward from 50 to the highest request (90), then continue to the outermost cylinder (199), then reverse to serve the remaining lower requests (39, 18).
examples.answer: FCFS total movement 120 cylinders, average 24 cylinders; SCAN total movement 330 cylinders, average 66 cylinders.
examples.check:
head = 50
requests = [55,58,39,18,90]
# FCFS
total_fcfs = sum(abs(requests[i] - (head if i==0 else requests[i-1])) for i in range(len(requests)))
avg_fcfs = total_fcfs / len(requests)
# SCAN (outward then to max cylinder 199 and back)
seq = [55,58,90,199,39,18]
prev = head
total_scan = 0
for r in seq:
    total_scan += abs(r - prev)
    prev = r
avg_scan = total_scan / len(requests)
print(total_fcfs)
print(total_scan)
print(avg_fcfs)
print(avg_scan)

traps: Adding the distance from the initial head position to the first request is often omitted, giving a lower total movement.
Confusing SCAN with C‑SCAN: C‑SCAN jumps back to the start without servicing, changing the total distance.
Treating cylinder numbers as sectors; cylinders are groups of tracks, not individual data blocks.
Using the maximum possible rotational latency (full rotation) instead of the average (half rotation) when computing access time.
Assuming seek time is constant for any distance; in reality it grows with the number of cylinders crossed.

quiz.q: What is a cylinder in the context of a magnetic disk?
quiz.a: A set of tracks that lie on the same radius on all platters.

quiz.q: Explain why the average rotational latency of a 5400 rpm disk is about 5.56 ms.
quiz.a: One full rotation takes 60 s ÷ 5400 rpm = 11.11 ms; on average the desired sector is half a rotation away, so 11.11 ms ÷ 2 ≈ 5.56 ms.

quiz.q: Given a request queue at cylinders 120, 30, 75 and a current head at 60, compute the total head movement for FCFS.
For the same queue (120, 30, 75) and head at 60, what is the total movement using SSTF?
quiz.a: Nearest to 60 is 75 (15), then 120 (45), then 30 (90). Total = 15+45+90 = 150 cylinders.

quiz.q: Compare FCFS and SCAN in terms of fairness and average seek time.
quiz.a: FCFS treats all requests equally in order of arrival, but can cause long seeks for late requests. SCAN provides more uniform wait times because the head sweeps the entire disk, reducing average seek but may delay requests near the ends until the sweep reaches them.

quiz.q: Name two variants of the elevator algorithm.
Why does C‑SCAN give better response time predictability than SCAN?
quiz.a: Because after reaching the last request, the head jumps back to the start without servicing any request, making the distance between two consecutive services roughly equal for all cylinders.

quiz.q: A disk rotates at 7200 rpm and has 200 sectors per track. How many milliseconds does it take, on average, to wait for a specific sector?
quiz.a: One rotation = 60 s ÷ 7200 = 8.33 ms. Average wait = half rotation = 4.17 ms.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern SSDs replace mechanical seeks with electronic page reads, but the scheduling concepts still apply to I/O queue management in the OS. Research on NVMe controllers explores multi‑queue scheduling to exploit parallelism, extending ideas from SCAN to per‑core queues. Cloud storage services use similar algorithms to balance latency across thousands of disks. Learning about request batching and deadline‑driven scheduling prepares you for performance‑critical applications like high‑frequency trading platforms. Search for "I/O elevator algorithm in Linux" and "deadline scheduler" to see current implementations.
